lead: A compiler does not translate a program in one jump. It pushes the program through a pipeline of phases, and each phase changes the representation: characters become tokens, tokens become a tree, the tree becomes machine-independent instructions, and those become target instructions. The pipeline exists because the whole job is too big for one step, and because the front half depends on the source language while the back half depends on the machine. GCC, javac and a small student compiler all follow this shape, sometimes with several phases merged into one pass.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1, which explains what a compiler is and how it differs from an interpreter and an assembler.

blocks.text: The input is a string of characters, the output is a string of machine instructions. In between, the compiler keeps rewriting the program into a form that is easier to work on. Read the phases in the order a source file meets them.

items: Lexical analysis reads characters and produces tokens, the smallest meaningful units: an identifier, a keyword, an operator, a constant. Full detail is in Chapter 1.4.
Syntax analysis, or parsing, checks the token stream against the grammar and builds a parse tree. See Unit 2, Syntax Analysis and Top-Down Parsing.
Semantic analysis checks meaning: every name is declared, types match, scope rules hold. It also inserts conversions such as int to float. See Unit 4.
Intermediate code generation turns the tree into simple machine-independent instructions, usually three-address code of the form x = y op z.
Optimization rewrites the intermediate code to run faster or use less memory while keeping the same meaning. See Unit 6.
Code generation maps intermediate code to the target machine: instruction selection, register use and addressing modes.
Machine-dependent optimization improves target code using facts about the machine, for example deleting a load that repeats the previous one.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call the intermediate code the intermediate representation, or IR. The optimizer and the code generator both read it, which is why it is the natural boundary between the two halves of the compiler.

sections.h3: The symbol table and the error handler serve every phase

blocks.text: Two components cut across the pipeline. Neither one is a phase: they are shared services that every phase calls.

items: Symbol table manager. The table keeps one record per name: the name itself, its type, its scope, its storage location and the line where it was declared. The lexer inserts identifier names, semantic analysis fills in types, code generation reads the address. Unit 5 covers the table in full.

Error handler. Each phase detects its own kind of error and reports it with a line number, then repairs just enough to continue. The lexer skips a bad character, the parser drops tokens until a safe symbol, semantic analysis records a type mismatch and carries on. A compiler that gives up at the first error annoys every programmer who uses it.

blocks.text: One shared symbol table keeps all phases agreeing on what a name means, so the type recorded by semantic analysis is exactly the type the code generator acts on.

sections.h3: Grouping the phases: front end and back end

blocks.text: The phases split into two halves at the intermediate code. The front end is also called analysis: lexical, syntax and semantic analysis plus intermediate code generation. It depends on the source language and not on the machine, so one front end can feed many targets. The back end is also called synthesis: optimization, code generation and machine-dependent optimization. It depends on the target machine and not on the source language, so one back end can serve many languages.

Single pass or many passes. A single-pass compiler interleaves the phases and reads the source once: the parser asks the lexer for the next token, and code is emitted as each construct is recognised. It is fast and needs little memory, but it never sees the whole program, so it optimizes weakly and struggles when a name is used before it is declared. A multi-pass compiler runs each phase to completion, stores the intermediate code, then optimizes. Most modern compilers are multi-pass, because memory is cheap and optimization matters.

figure.caption: The program is rewritten at every stage, and the token stream from lexical analysis is the first form that is no longer raw text. A correct compiler may skip only the optimizer.

spec.title: Phases of a compiler
spec.aria: The source passes through lexical, syntax, semantic, intermediate code, optimizer and code generator stages to produce target code.

examples.question: Trace the assignment position = initial + rate * 60 through all phases of a compiler. Show the token stream, the shape of the parse tree, the three-address code and what the optimizer does to it.
steps: Lexical analysis groups the characters into 7 tokens: id1 = id2 + id3 * 60, where id1 is position, id2 is initial, id3 is rate, and 60 is a constant. The operators =, + and * are tokens too.

Syntax analysis builds the tree from the grammar and operator precedence. The root is =, with id1 as its left child. The right child of = is +; the children of + are id2 and *; the children of * are id3 and 60. Multiplication sits below addition because it binds tighter.

Semantic analysis looks up id1, id2 and id3 in the symbol table and finds all three declared as float. The integer 60 is widened to the real constant 60.0. The expression type is float and the assignment is type-correct, so no error is reported.
Intermediate code generation emits three-address code with 2 temporaries: t1 = id3 * 60.0; t2 = id2 + t1; id1 = t2. That is 3 instructions.
Optimization checks for common subexpressions, dead code and constant folding. There is none: t1 and t2 are each used once, and 60.0 cannot be folded with an unknown value. The code stays the same.
Code generation picks instructions and registers. One possible output: LD R1, rate; MUL R1, R1, #60.0; LD R2, initial; ADD R1, R2, R1; ST position, R1.
examples.answer: The assignment produces 7 tokens, 2 temporaries and 3 three-address instructions, and the optimizer leaves the code unchanged because there is no common subexpression to remove.
examples.check:
tokens = ["id1", "=", "id2", "+", "id3", "*", "60"]
print(len(tokens))
ops = [t for t in tokens if t in ("+", "*")]
print(len(ops))
print(len(ops) + 1)
print(int(tokens[-1]))

traps: Phases are logical stages, not always separate programs. A real compiler may merge lexical and syntax analysis, or optimization and code generation, into one pass.
The symbol table and the error handler are not phases. They are shared tables and routines that every phase uses, and examiners often ask you to place them in the diagram.
The optimizer must not change the meaning of the program. It is also optional for correctness: a simple compiler that skips it still produces a correct target program.
Front end versus back end is about language dependence and machine dependence. Do not mix it up with the order of execution in a single-pass compiler, where the phases run interleaved.
A common slip: saying the parser removes comments and whitespace. The lexical analyzer does that; the parser never sees comments or spaces.

quiz.q: List the phases of a compiler in the order a source file passes through them.
quiz.a: Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, optimization, code generation, machine-dependent optimization.

quiz.q: Name the two components that every phase uses.
quiz.a: The symbol table manager and the error handler.

quiz.q: Why can a front end be reused when the target machine changes, while a back end cannot?
quiz.a: The front end works only with source-language facts, so it is machine independent and its intermediate code is portable. The back end encodes registers, addressing modes and instruction selection of one machine, so it must be rebuilt for a new target.

quiz.q: Why does a single-pass compiler optimize weakly?
quiz.a: It reads the source once and emits code as it parses, so it never holds the whole program. It cannot compare code from far-apart regions, cannot look ahead to a later declaration, and cannot run global passes over the intermediate code.

quiz.q: Write three-address code for z = a * (b + c) and state the number of temporaries.
quiz.a: t1 = b + c; t2 = a * t1; z = t2. Two temporaries, t1 and t2, and three instructions. The brackets are honoured because b + c is computed first.

quiz.q: A language lets a name be used before it is declared. Would you choose a single-pass or a multi-pass compiler, and why?
quiz.a: Multi-pass. A single pass sees the use before the declaration record exists in the symbol table and cannot fill the type. A multi-pass compiler finishes the declaration pass first, or patches the reference later.

quiz.q: A compiler deliberately skips the optimizer. Which property of the output is lost and which is kept?
quiz.a: Correctness is kept: the target program still computes the same results. What is lost is efficiency, meaning fewer instructions, fewer registers and less memory traffic, so the program runs slower than an optimized build.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production compilers separate the intermediate representation into a reusable layer: LLVM IR sits between many front ends and many targets, and MLIR generalises this idea to several levels of IR that can be lowered step by step. The JVM and modern JavaScript engines use tiered compilation, which is a fast single-pass style tier followed by multi-pass optimizing tiers for hot code. Compiler correctness work also leans on this structure, since each phase boundary is a place where a verifier can check the representation. Useful search terms: LLVM IR, MLIR, tiered JIT compilation.
